item.content:encoded:
I see a large amount of heavy criticism in these discussion posts, but it wasn't bad.

The SCP's aren't required to be the most terrifying thing ever, just strange and otherworldly.

Admittedly, the "SCPs don't have to be scary to be successful" mindset is a lot more widespread now than it was when this piece was originally posted, back in 2009.

That said, I do like this piece a lot. It was one of the first pieces I read before I joined.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I see a large amount of heavy criticism in these discussion posts, but it wasn't bad. The addition of papers that represent a threat to the security and secrecy of the Foundation is also entertaining.
From what I could tell, the largest gripe concerning this so far is the lack of a sense of danger as "paper cuts aren't scary enough", which I discard immediately. The SCP's aren't required to be the most terrifying thing ever, just strange and otherworldly. I think the author has succeeded in doing so, possibly with a few too many words in one area and not enough in another, which was another complaint, but that isn't a terribly huge issue.
The information provided makes me curious as to how this came to be, and despite my desire for an explanation, I think it does better without. The mystery and the desire to know more has earned my up vote.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Fantastic concept, and I think, aside from needing a slight upgrade in tone, it stands as it is quite well. Could stand to have a few less redactions, I suppose, but that's what four years will do to an article. Really, this has that sense of wonder I'm always looking for in skips. And honestly, Re: all the criticism about papercuts upthread, how else is paper gonna defend itself? To the paper, those cuts mean it's being serious, that's hardcore, man, don't mess with paper! Marvelous.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Honestly, I think the tone is basically fine, even if it's sort of antiquated. I could buy this as a document produced by professionals, for use by other professionals. The redaction, apart from that in the containment, could theoretically be toned down a bit, but I don't see a compelling reason to do so.

The redaction in the containment procedures, though, really is silly. Requesting permission to change "every ██ days" to "every two weeks" and "fewer than █ pages" to "fewer than five" — both pulled out of my ass, but both far more acceptable than blackboxing.

Since collection of SCP-211-1 has begun, several specific books have become identified as their origin. Examples of these are as follows:

A 19██ copy of Hitler's Mein Kampf, found in ████████ Public Library.
A Java Data Structures Book, printed in 19██, discovered in a used book store near Site-17.
[REDACTED], currently stored in the United States Library of Congress.
Three printouts of Japanese broadcasts decoded during the MAGIC Cryptanalysis Project in World War II.
The drawing in Document-211-02.
etc.
No documents re: the Foundation have been discovered as of yet; however, security has been increased as a mild informational security threat.

What? "etc."? "No documents re:"? What is going on with the ending here?

item.content:encoded:
I would say to have the "paper-cuts" be an escalating response; like, you mess with the paper once, they cut you a little, you mess with it again, they drop a stack of cuts on you, you mess with it again (like trying to burn the house down), they do what they did to the bulldozer.

You could have something like: "at this point SCP-211-1 was observed to [DATA REDACTED] oozing down the walls, though some fragments were not recovered, and [DATA REDACTED] the remains later vanished mysteriously, but no reports of cleaning crews entering the building were filed. Upon examination the next day, the papers covering the fence to the backyard were found to have spread approx. 1 meter onto the grass from their previous end-point."

So, like, the house ate the people's remains and used it to grow more papers… or something. >_> You could have it mentioned in the article that the papers started in one part of the house, but each time it killed someone, they spread.
